inline.s: Excerpted from the Miraculous Record of the Living Buddha of Jinshan

There are many people in the world who delight in the pastime of physiognomy and fortune-telling. We Chinese women, in particular, are especially superstitious about such things. There are often women who are extremely stingy and would not part with a single hair, yet when it comes to a fortune-teller they do not begrudge the expense. In their hearts, whether the matter is great or small, they cannot feel at ease until they have consulted the fortune-teller. It is as if everything were fixed by destiny, and only the fortune-teller knows one's fate. Those who harbor such foolish fancies are beyond number!

I remember that when the Living Buddha and I were staying at the Hu family's home in Nanjing, old Mrs. Hu was the most superstitious of all about physiognomy and fortune-telling, and she would constantly run over to the Confucius Temple to have the fortunes of her sons and daughters-in-law told. At that time there was a famous physiognomist and fortune-teller at the Confucius Temple known as "Iron Abacus." People generally said that the fortunes this "Iron Abacus" read and calculated were uncannily accurate, describing him practically as a living immortal. And so the officials and nobles and their wives and daughters of the day all delighted in seeking out "Iron Abacus" for a reading. Old Mrs. Hu was naturally one of "Iron Abacus's" regular patrons. Every time she returned from having a fortune told, she would, as usual, recount it to the family, telling it vividly and with relish. When she came to the good parts, her brows lifted and her face broke into a smile, as if a golden ingot would drop from the sky tomorrow and she would become a great millionaire; when she came to the bad parts, she sighed and lamented, as if calamity were about to descend upon the house.

Once, old Mrs. Hu's eldest grandson, Hu Dadong, was preparing to become engaged. For such a great matter, she of course had to run over to "Iron Abacus" to have it calculated, to see whether his fate matched that of the girl. She returned from the reading overjoyed. She had heard from "Iron Abacus" that the two of them, by their "eight characters," were a match made in heaven, of unsurpassed nobility, and that in the future they would bear five sons and two daughters — a true "reunion of seven children" — with wealth, honor, longevity, and endless blessings. Now "Iron Abacus's" rule was to charge five yuan for reading the "yearly fortune" and ten yuan for evaluating the "eight characters." Because old Mrs. Hu heard that her grandson's fiancée's "eight characters" were so excellent, in a moment of delight she took out an extra ten yuan and gave it to "Iron Abacus" for tea (so he truly proved to be an iron abacus).

As old Mrs. Hu recounted the fortune-telling, the Living Buddha and I sat beside her listening quietly. When old Mrs. Hu had finished, the Living Buddha let out a laugh and said: "I can tell fortunes too!" Everyone thought he was joking. A moment later, the Living Buddha put on a serious look and said: "I truly can tell fortunes." Old Mrs. Hu laughed and said: "Well then, let me tell you my eight characters, and ask the Living Buddha to calculate how this old life of mine will turn out."

We only heard the Living Buddha say, as if in jest: "I do not care to calculate the fortunes of one or two people; I want to calculate the fortunes of the many — best of all, hand over the fortunes of everyone under heaven to me to calculate..." Before he had finished, old Mrs. Hu at once asked: "What do you mean by that? How do you calculate?" The Living Buddha said: "Naturally there is a principle to it, and naturally I have my own way of calculating. Those fortune-tellers think that the people of the world each have their own fate, each different from the rest. In my view, there are not two kinds. Not only is one person's fate the same as another's, even the fate of the birds and beasts, down to the fish and insects, is no different from that of humans. It is only in outward appearance that they differ." Old Mrs. Hu cried out: "Living Buddha, the more you say the more mysterious it gets — how could there be such a thing!" The Living Buddha said: "Truly! Truly!" Old Mrs. Hu laughed and said: "Well then, calculate the fate of the people of the world!" The Living Buddha nodded and said: "Easy! Easy! If you want me to calculate, I will calculate." With that, he closed both eyes and said no more, with much the air of a storyteller who, just at the critical point, rises and steps down from the stage.

At this everyone grew anxious and cried: "Living Buddha, calculate then!" After a moment the Living Buddha opened his eyes and said very seriously: "When I calculate a fortune, I do not arrange the eight characters — jia, yi, bing, ding, wu, ji, geng, xin. When I calculate a person's fate, there is only one character, and that character is called 'karma.' What ordinary people call 'destiny,' the Buddha calls 'karmic conditions.'"

You all think that this thing which can speak, dress, eat, and walk is life; the Buddha calls it the 'reward-body.' Because of the karma created in the past, there is now this body that receives the reward. Karma is of two kinds: 'pure karma' and 'defiled karma.' 'Pure karma' is good karma, and 'defiled karma' is evil karma. The good karma created in the past brings good reward now; the evil karma created brings evil reward now. If one has both good and evil karma from the past, then now one receives both retribution and blessing. The power of good and evil karma follows one like a shadow, never erring in the slightest." The Living Buddha continued: "The people of the world are all human alike; why do some enjoy blessings while others suffer? This is because each person's past karma differs. Not only does each person's past karma differ, even children born of the same mother meet with different fortunes. In appearance too there are the handsome and the ugly; in temperament there are the good and the bad; and in conduct and behavior there is every variety. How is it that a handsome couple gives birth to ugly children, while some parents who are very ugly have children who grow up perfectly proper? This is because the karma each created in the past differs, and so the reward received now is also not the same."

The Living Buddha paused for a moment, then said again: "This 'karma' does not come from outside, nor does it arise of itself; it is entirely within, and it is entirely created by oneself..." Old Mrs. Hu asked: "Is it the eyes that create karma? The hands that create karma? The nose that create karma?" The Living Buddha laughed and said: "Not at all. The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body cannot create 'karma'; what can create 'karma' is your own 'mind.' Everything is created by 'mind' alone. For example, you, old Mrs. Hu, know how to paint. In the past you delighted in painting landscapes, and now you delight in painting images of Guanyin — all of this is turned by your 'mind,' and the hand that paints is merely directed by your 'mind.' If your 'mind' does not wish to paint, the hand cannot produce anything either. The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body are all the same in principle. If the 'mind' does not wish to see anything, the eyes will not perceive the scenes and colors outside; if the 'mind' does not wish to hear anything, the ears will not hear the sounds; if the 'mind' does not wish to smell anything, the nose will not discern fragrant or foul odors; if the 'mind' does not give rise to distinctions, the body will not know cold or warmth, coarseness or fineness. Everything is ruled by the 'mind'; everything is directed by the 'mind.'"

Having spoken to this point, the Living Buddha feared that if he went any deeper old Mrs. Hu would not understand, so he changed the subject and said: "The people of the world all hope for wealth, honor, longevity, and many sons and grandsons. Little do they know that sons and grandsons are all accumulated through cultivation in past lives; they are not accidental, cannot be known in advance, and cannot be obtained by seeking. With good deeds in a past life, one naturally enjoys blessings and long life in this one. With the karmic affinity of children from a past life, one will naturally have children in this one. They will come of themselves; even if you do not want them, they will come, and when they come, they cannot be stopped. Without the affinity of children, no matter how you seek them, you will not obtain them. If you wish to know what 'karma' you created in your past life, you may understand it through what you receive in this one. If you ask how your future will turn out, then look at how your thoughts arise and move right now. If you understand this principle, then you can do without fortune-telling."

Having spoken to this point, the Living Buddha let out a long laugh: "How it makes me laugh!" Everyone asked: "Laugh at what?" The Living Buddha said: "I laugh at how the people of the world are born in confusion and die in confusion, not one of them knowing his own fate — what he did in his past life, whether it was good or evil. I laugh even more at those fortune-tellers: they do not even recognize their own origins, conditions, and outcome, so how can they recognize other people's destinies, or dare to predict the good and bad fortune of others' futures? Since none understands the 'karma' he created in the past, I ask you: from where does one begin to calculate this fate? How does one calculate it? How can it be calculated through? How can it be calculated clearly?" With that the Living Buddha clapped his hands and cried: "Old Mrs. Hu! This business of fortune-telling is a trick by which wandering charlatans cheat people of their money; it cannot be believed. I tell you: the only one who truly knows how to tell fortunes is Shakyamuni Buddha. Only he knows the causes and conditions of the birth, death, transgressions, blessings, and retributions of the beings of this great earth. Those who believe in and study the Buddha must believe the Buddha's words; do not have your fortune told — only ask about your present mind." Hearing these words of the Living Buddha, old Mrs. Hu came to realize that the two characters "destiny" and "fortune" could not be relied upon, and that one ought to believe in the "power of karma." She sighed and said: "Living Buddha, your words have awakened me. Had I heard them earlier, I would not have made a fool of myself and spent all that money on fortune-telling!" Everyone burst into laughter.

That time when the Living Buddha spoke on destiny, his words pointed out the truth of life taught in Buddhism. His meaning was to tell people not to believe in "destiny," but to believe in "karma"; to teach people not to create evil karma but to create more good karma, and good results will come of themselves. There is a Chinese proverb: "Only do good deeds, and ask not about the road ahead" — precisely this.
